analysis.one_liner: Bans making, using, and selling asbestos, with a short phase-out for chlorine plants.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: introduced with no cosponsors, it received a hearing but never a committee vote, and expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Asbestos causes cancer, and the United States still allows it to be imported and used in a handful of products, mainly by chemical plants that make chlorine. This bill would make it illegal to manufacture, process, use, or sell commercial asbestos one year after enactment, give chlorine plants two years to switch to alternatives, and require companies that handle asbestos to report who was exposed. It never got a vote in the committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in plants and demolition sites, people living near facilities that use asbestos, and the general public, who would face less exposure to a known carcinogen. Families of asbestos-disease victims, for whom the bill is named, would see the remaining legal uses of asbestos end.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and anyone exposed to asbestos

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits manufacturing, processing, using, or selling commercial asbestos and any product containing it, effective one year after enactment [S3].
Gives chlorine plants that use asbestos diaphragms a two-year window to keep importing and using asbestos fibers while they switch to alternatives [S3].
Requires any company that handled asbestos to report within months where it was used, how much, and how many people were exposed, with the reports made public [S3].
Excludes asbestos already installed in buildings from the ban and permits its disposal under existing rules, so the ban targets new uses rather than penalizing homeowners [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The chlor-alkali (chlorine production) industry, which would have to replace asbestos-based equipment within two years, and the small number of importers and manufacturers still using asbestos, who bear switching and disposal costs. Consumers could see small price effects on chlorine-based products during the transition.

drawbacks.text: The industry argues alternatives to asbestos diaphragms in chlorine production are costly to retrofit, which is why the bill's two-year phase-out was written narrowly to cover only plants already in operation [S3].
The ban does nothing about asbestos already in walls, ceilings, and pipes in older buildings; it only exempts existing installations from the new prohibition and leaves abatement to other law [S3].
The President could exempt a company from the ban on national security grounds for up to six years, with terms that only require the maximum practicable exposure reduction [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health gain — ending the remaining legal uses of a carcinogen that kills tens of thousands of Americans a year — far outweighs the transition cost to a small number of chlorine plants, which were given two years to convert. The bill's main weakness is not its design but that it never got the chance to be debated, amended, or voted on.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, got one subcommittee hearing, and sat there until the two-year Congress ended without a committee vote or floor action.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on May 18, 2022, with no cosponsors [S1, S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S5].
A subcommittee on chemical safety held a hearing on the bill on June 9, 2022, but the full committee never voted to advance it [S5].
No further action occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill expired [S5, S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The chlor-alkali industry and the remaining importers and users of asbestos are better off: they can keep importing and using asbestos with no new restrictions. Workers and the public remain exposed to a known carcinogen that Congress declined to act on.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and the only senator to sponsor it; it never advanced past a subcommittee hearing.

against.name: Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.role: Senate committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, held one subcommittee hearing, and never scheduled a committee vote or reported the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. A single Democrat sponsored the bill, no Republicans or other Democrats signed on, and no roll-call record exists to show where the parties stood.

industries.note: These plants are the main remaining U.S. users of asbestos, importing processed fibers to make chlorine-production diaphragms. The bill would have forced them off asbestos within two years; they continued using it because the bill died.

industries.industry: Asbestos importers, processors, and product makers
industries.note: Any company manufacturing, processing, using, or selling asbestos-containing products would have had to stop within a year and file detailed exposure reports. With the bill dead, these uses remain legal.

A ban would have eventually shifted activity toward removal of existing asbestos and safe disposal, work that a phase-down generally expands. This is a modest, speculative effect since the bill never advanced.
